title: why monks don't beg
hook: a shaved head, a simple robe, a bowl at dawn: what the alms round really is

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four noble truths, a diagnosis, not a verdict. Today, the people who give their whole lives to the fourth one.

Dawn in a town in Thailand or Laos. A line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot down the street, heads shaved, each carrying a covered bowl. People kneel on mats by the curb with pots of rice. The monks don't ask for anything. And the people giving are often the ones who bow. To an outsider it can look like begging. It isn't, and the difference is today's word.
screen: `DAWN. A LINE OF MONKS.` → `THEY DON'T ASK.` → `THE GIVERS BOW.`

segments.voice: Dana means giving. Start with the monks. The shaved head and the simple robe go back to the Buddha's own leaving home: the story says he cut off his hair with his sword. Shaving it lets go of vanity, a way of saying: I'm not dressing for anyone. Traditionally a monk owns almost nothing: robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a few small things. In the Theravada tradition, monks don't eat after midday. That's a training rule for monastics, not a fast everyone keeps. And their food comes from giving. So the alms round isn't begging; it's an exchange. The monk gets a meal. The giver practices dana, which many Buddhists understand as making merit: good karma, and a lighter heart. When the Buddha met people who'd never heard him teach, the texts say he often started with giving, before anything else. In many East Asian monasteries, monks and nuns cook and farm for themselves, and lay people give in other ways. The open hand is the same.
screen: `THE SHAVED HEAD, THE SIMPLE ROBE` · `A BOWL, A RAZOR, A NEEDLE` · `NOTHING AFTER MIDDAY` · `NOT BEGGING: GIVING` · then, large: `GIVE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. On the first breath, notice what an open hand feels like. On the second, think of one thing you could give that isn't money: time, attention, a kind word. On the third, picture someone receiving it.
Dana. Giving: what fills the monk's bowl, and the first practice the Buddha taught. Fifth word.
Your line: give first. In the old order of teaching, the open hand came before everything else. That's day five.

screen: `DAY 5 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ONE FULL MOON, THREE STORIES.`

howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food, robes and medicine to monks and nuns, most visibly on the morning alms round in Theravada countries and at temple meals (in Sri Lanka, families 'give a dana'), and by giving to others in daily life; some meditation teachers teach freely on a dana basis.

fork.reveal: giving came first, then good conduct. the deeper teachings came once the listener was ready.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, a gift. The first of the perfections (pāramī).

trapdoor: what you thought: monks begging for food.
what it means: an exchange of gifts: the monk gets a meal, the giver practices generosity, the first practice of the path.

what a scholar hears: dāna opens the anupubbī-kathā, the gradual talk, and heads the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana lists; eating at the wrong time (after midday) is a Vinaya offense for monastics.

story.title: the prince's first meal
story.text: A prince who has only ever eaten off gold plates walks into a city with a clay bowl, asking for nothing, and takes whatever people put in it. When he sits down to eat the cold, mixed scraps, his stomach turns. The story says he spoke to himself: you saw a wandering monk and wished for this life, and now you have it. Then he ate. It was the first meal of the man who would become the Buddha.
story.source: the Nidanakatha, a later telling of the Buddha's life (introduction to the Jataka)

wrong.truth: on the alms round they don't ask. people give, and giving, dana, is a practice for the giver too.

notes: Moved from day 14 (dana) to day 5 and reworked around the audience research's 'monks: the shaved head, the robes, the food' and 'why we give monks food (merit, not begging)'. The giving teaching is kept; the Dhammapada 223 quotation and the perfections detail were cut to keep it to one idea (the perfections stay in the trapdoor).
Monks' requisites given as 'robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a few small things' (the traditional eight requisites also include a belt and a water strainer). Confirm.
Not eating after midday: the Vinaya rule (Pacittiya 37) is stated for 'the Theravada tradition'; East Asian monastic practice varies (e.g., an evening 'medicine meal'). Confirm.
'Many Buddhists understand [giving] as making merit: good karma, and a lighter heart.' Confirm the plain-English gloss of puñña.
The cut hair (Nidanakatha) and the first alms meal at Rajagaha, where his stomach turned and he admonished himself, are from later biographies, told as 'the story says'. Confirm details.
East Asian monasteries 'cook and farm for themselves' (the Chan/Zen work tradition): stated generally. Confirm.
Sri Lankan English 'give a dana' (a meal offered to monks) is in howItsDone; confirm with a Sri Lankan Keeper.
